newsitem.title: UK: W.African crude attractive, Med markets listless.
newsitem.headline: W.African crude attractive, Med markets listless.

text.p: West African crudes were priced steady to higher on Thursday and being actively sought into the third decade of August, traders said.
In the Mediterranean the absence of Iraqi barrels continued to offer background support, with Russian Urals thinly supplied, but smaller parcels were on offer.

A third decade August cargo of Escravos was heard traded on Thursday in the low 40s above dated Brent from a U.S. equity holder to a U.S. refiner. Dealers said the trade was indicative of the slightly stronger numbers being achieved.

"There is enough buying from Asia to keep prices in west Africa solid, along with the U.S. and Med demand," said one trader. He believed most first and second decade cargoes were already spoken for, with third decade thinning out.
"Unusually we haven't seen any distressed cargoes like we did up to two months ago when the peaks of demand and supply didn't coincide," he added.
"So what we're seeing is decent buying, but not a scramble, with largely stable premiums for some weeks."

But Asian demand is less than at its spectacular peak when July barrels were swept up. Estimated demand is reckoned at 30 to 50 percent down from the 1.5 million barrels per day purchased from the July programme.
Far Eastern buyers as usual were said to prefer heavy, sweet Angolan crudes.

A Cabinda/Nembe loading 19-20 August changed hands on Wednesday, with the first element moving at dated Brent plus $1.05 and the second part traded at dated +4 cents. A Brass River was heard swapped for a Gabonese Rabi by two majors.
Bonny Light was assessed at dated +48-51 cents, Qua Iboe at dated +43-46 cents, Escravos at +40-43 cents and Forcados at dated +25-30 cents.
Mediterranean values were opaque, with numbers in the 70s and 80s below dated Brent mentioned for Russian Urals barrels.
Trade was sluggish, with most hoping Iraqi barrels would return to the market in time to prevent them needing to make big purchases.

A trader was heard to have moved a Urals cargo he bought on Tuesday to a regional refiner for "a number in the 70s" below dated Brent, while another trader was offering 130,000 tonnes aboard the Marina M for roughly the same amount.
Small cargoes were still on offer for late July and availability eases dramatically into August, in anticipation of the return of Kirkuk blend.
